r.title: Prepare the environment and identify the installation
r.goal: Check whether an external participant can prepare and open the supplied candidate using the documentation.
steps: Agree on the R participant profile, basic/full technical level and five-type core/seven-constructor scope. Record prior R, SQL and FHIR experience, existing dependencies and planned assistance.
Check the ZIP and CANDIDATO.json. Record package version, commit and SHA-256, operating system, architecture and R version. Separate dependency preparation time from candidate installation time.
Run INICIAR.R into a new directory and abrir_sesion() in a clean R session. Check packageVersion(), find.package(), help and vignettes.
Keep SESION.json and the original log; describe each obstacle and the documentation used.
checks: The supplied identity and the loaded installation were checked.
Environment, technical level and scope were recorded before the tasks.
Help and vignettes were located, or the obstacle was documented.
Preparation times and observer interventions were recorded separately.
questions: How would you check that R is using this candidate rather than another installed copy?
Which steps need network access, and which should work once dependencies are prepared?
r.expected: Version 0.5.0.9002 with the supplied commit and file hash; the session library is loaded. Full level needs DBI/DuckDB and R ≥ 4.2; basic needs R ≥ 4.1. Finding documentation independently is not an observer intervention.
r.evidence: SESION.json, candidato.txt, reviewed library location, versions and preparation log.
r.mistakes: Confusing version with file identity; loading another library; including network waits in analysis time.
r.code:
source("INICIAR.R")
iniciar_piloto("basico", "sesion-P01-intento01")
abrir_sesion("sesion-P01-intento01")
packageVersion("fhirviews")
find.package("fhirviews")
help("fhir_mapa", package = "fhirviews")
browseVignettes("fhirviews")

r.title: Interpret checks and surveillance indicators
r.goal: Explain what the trial measures and identify an incorrect epidemiological interpretation.
steps: Open aceptacion.json and aceptacion.csv. Locate identity, schema, checks, warnings and findings without editing the reports.
Explain what each check demonstrates and what is not evaluated at the chosen level. Check totals and event exclusions against the fictional files.
Follow den-c0001 to its patient and residence; check that den-c0002 is absent from confirmed events. Review at least one territorial and one monthly count in the example outputs.
Describe the unit of analysis and the additional information needed to count unique people or calculate a population rate.
checks: The five checks, exclusions and warnings were interpreted.
Totals and an included/excluded event were checked against evidence.
One territorial and one monthly aggregation were reviewed.
Events, people and rates were distinguished, and limitations were written down.
questions: Can every output row be interpreted as a different person? Why?
Does an automatic pass demonstrate unassisted use by another person or validation against a national profile?
r.expected: 755 input events, 661 confirmed, 94 excluded and 65 cantons. den-c0001→den-p0001, residence 0701, onset 2025-02-27; den-c0002 excluded. Canton 0701: 55 events; February: 73. These are fictional event counts; a rate needs a compatible denominator and period. Basic: recovery not evaluated; full: five checks passed.
r.evidence: Original report and interpretation note identifying the rows or fields checked.
r.mistakes: Turning counts into rates; counting events as patients; treating not evaluated as passed.

r.title: Trace a table back to its R4 sources
r.goal: Relate tables to resources and explain keys, missing values and precision.
steps: Open the six resources in piloto/r4/recursos-r4.ndjson and create a local type/id/relevant references table.
Follow Patient, Encounter, Condition, Observation and Immunization; compare at least one table row with its NDJSON line.
Compare false, an absent field and NA; locate both immunizations’ occurrence and dose-number alternatives.
Inspect decimal literals in the file and explain what is lost if the SQL source supplies them as double.
checks: The number of types, resources and output rows were distinguished.
The selected row’s keys and references were traced to their sources.
FALSE, absence and NA were explained without filling in data.
Scale was checked in JSON as well as in the R table.
questions: Why does a table printing 72 not demonstrate preservation of the literal 72.00?
What is the risk of filling in an unknown date or joining tables only by row order?
r.expected: Five types and six resources: p1/e1/c1/o1/i1/i2. Condition/c1 and Immunization/i1 reference Encounter/e1; both immunizations reference Patient/p1. active=false is present information. i2 has no encounter or quantity and retains textual date/dose alternatives. 72.00 and 0.50 have lower boundaries 71.995 and 0.495.
r.evidence: Local provenance table, references and reviewed fictional JSON fragments.
r.mistakes: Confusing false with absence; losing trailing zeros before mapping; inventing a date, quantity or patient.

r.title: Build new resources and understand errors
r.goal: Create a small mapping with fictional data and resolve an error using the help.
steps: Write a script with two new fictional Patient rows: distinct ids, valid gender, birthDate and logical active, including FALSE. Consult fhir_mapa(), fhir_desde_tabla() and fhir_escribir().
Build resources using an explicit map, write NDJSON and read it again. Check both records and retain the script, map and output.
In separate data copies, duplicate an id and use an invalid gender. Capture each rejection and explain how to correct the source without hiding the error.
At full level, repeat the valid case using a DuckDB table and a parameterized query selecting one id. Compare outputs and close the connection. At basic level, record that DBI was not evaluated.
checks: The valid case was built, saved and reread with its explicit values.
Both invalid inputs were rejected and their diagnostics were retained.
The source correction was explained and made in a new copy.
The DBI path was checked at full level or explicitly excluded at basic level.
questions: What does one input row mean to this constructor, and how would you prepare two rows with the same id?
When would you use SQL parameters, and what would you do if a large identifier arrived rounded?
r.expected: Two valid Patient resources retain their ids and active=FALSE. Duplicate ids and gender outside the required binding produce fhirviews_error_mapeo. Ids are not grouped or silently overwritten. DBI uses WHERE id = ? with parametros=list(...), and CAST to text when source precision requires it. Local construction does not demonstrate profile validation.
r.evidence: Participant script, valid NDJSON, diagnostics for both negative cases and DBI comparison when applicable.
r.mistakes: Using the text "false" as a logical value; deleting rows merely to obtain a pass; interpolating values into SQL.

r.title: Design, modify and reuse a view
r.goal: Solve a new extraction task using documentation and verify its meaning.
steps: Create an Immunization view with status, patient and date from the trial NDJSON; retain the definition before extending it.
Add columns for both occurrence alternatives and save a second JSON definition. Run it and explain every NA using the original resources.
Read the saved definition with vista_leer() and repeat the extraction; check keys, values, types and counts without requiring row order unless agreed.
Describe a change for an analysis need of your own, using only the fictional data. Record documentation consulted and any supplied solution.
checks: Two JSON versions were retained and the second was reused.
Both immunizations remained correctly identified.
Missing alternatives and types were checked against NDJSON.
The participant explained the view and any assistance, beyond executing it.
questions: What must you save so another person can reproduce this extraction?
Which original information does your view leave out that another analysis might need?
r.expected: Two rows i1/i2 with patient key p1. Project occurrence.ofType(dateTime) and occurrence.ofType(string) separately; missing alternatives remain NA. The reread definition produces the same table and types. A ViewDefinition can omit information and is insufficient to reconstruct the complete resource.
r.evidence: vista-inmunizaciones-01.json, vista-inmunizaciones-02.json, tables and the participant’s explanation.
r.mistakes: Copying a solution and claiming independence; replacing NA; assuming a projection is reversible.

r.title: Analyze allergies while preserving the counting unit
r.goal: Avoid overcounting records when expanding reactions and manifestations.
steps: Locate the allergy NDJSON and execute the catalogue view. Compare nrow() with the number of distinct ids.
Group rows by id and reconstruct allergy→reaction→manifestation for a record with multiple rows.
Inspect an allergy with no reaction and its missing values. Identify multiple categories and distinguish criticality from reaction severity.
Explain which count you would report for recorded allergies and how it changes when counting manifestations. Retain the code and justification.
checks: Row and distinct-id counts were calculated separately.
Manifestations retained their own reaction and severity.
Allergies without reactions were retained in the analysis.
The counting unit and treatment of missing values and lists were justified.
questions: What error would result from using nrow(table) as the number of allergies?
Does an allergy with no documented reaction mean that no reaction occurred?
r.expected: Three ids and five rows: a1 has three manifestations in two reactions; a2 and a3 each retain a row without a reaction. Do not infer clinical absence from missing documentation. Categories remain lists. criticality and reaction.severity have different meanings.
r.evidence: Counting script, table by id and explanation of the unit of analysis.
r.mistakes: Counting rows as records; dropping allergies without reactions; assigning one severity to all manifestations.
r.code:
archivo <- system.file("extdata", "alergias_r4.ndjson", package = "fhirviews")
alergias <- vista_ejecutar(archivo, vista_plantilla("alergias"))
alergias[, c("id", "estado_clinico", "gravedad_reaccion", "reaccion_codigo")]
length(unique(alergias$id))

r.title: Repeat the analysis and examine recovery
r.goal: Check repeatability and document which tasks can be repeated without intervention.
steps: Run the agreed technical level again in a different directory, retaining both reports and the same candidate.
Compare findings and states; distinguish path/time differences from data/type differences.
Repeat view creation/reuse and allergy counting without observer hints. Identify the tasks and files supporting the repeat.
At full level, review recovery and explain rollback/retry without duplicates. At basic level, retain not evaluated and limit the conclusion.
checks: Both attempts and the candidate were identified.
Data, states and types were compared, with differences explained.
The manual repeat recorded scope, result and interventions.
Recovery was interpreted according to the technical level.
questions: Why does rerunning the automatic command alone not demonstrate that you can modify a view?
What would you check before retrying a load that failed halfway through?
r.expected: Findings match; paths and durations need not match. A full retry replaces the load after rollback without accumulating duplicates. Independence is limited to manual tasks actually repeated without assistance, with evidence of the second attempt.
r.evidence: Two reports, written comparison and manual-repeat files; describe any assistance.
r.mistakes: Overwriting the first attempt; comparing totals only; claiming independence from an automatic script.

r.title: Assess usefulness and agree on closure
r.goal: Decide what use was demonstrated and which improvements need follow-up.
steps: Review R01–R07 and R09 when applicable; log obstacles and interpretation errors with expected/observed behavior and evidence.
Answer the closing interview: usefulness for your own task, most confusing step, confidence interpreting outputs and up to three priority improvements. Distinguish opinion from measurement.
Participant and maintainer review the decision for the exact scope, excluded tasks, owners and next check. Critical/high issues require correction and retesting.
Export JSON, CSV and text; check that records can be reopened and agreed attachments are readable and contain no personal information.
checks: Usefulness was related to a specific task and its limitations.
Issues and priorities have evidence and an owner.
The human decision and unevaluated scopes were explicit.
Agreed exports and attachments were reviewed and retained.
questions: Which real task would you try next with this tool, and what prevents you from doing it today?
What would you need to check before recommending it to a colleague?
r.expected: Conclusions may request retesting after corrections, accept the stated scope, or accept with explicit minor follow-up. No favorable closure with incomplete required tasks, incorrect understanding or unverified critical/high issues. The session does not constitute clinical or institutional acceptance.
r.evidence: Reviewed exported record, experiencia-usuario.txt, issues and follow-up plan.
r.mistakes: Confusing satisfaction with correctness; closing an issue merely because code changed; omitting limitations.

r.title: Evaluate the laboratory path for seven constructors
r.goal: Complete SQL→R4 laboratory→tables when evaluating the seven-type scope.
steps: Confirm seven-type scope and full level; open the installed laboratorio-r4.R example and read inputs, maps and queries before execution.
Run laboratorio_r4() and write its resources to a new NDJSON. Identify types, ids and links between patient, specimen, observations and report.
Save the three views and compare V8/DuckDB tables by keys, values and types. Inspect volume/result scale in NDJSON.
Explain how to obtain one row per result and avoid counting a report twice. For core scope, mark not evaluated with a reason; do not claim evaluation of all seven types.
checks: The example ran from the verified installation using DBI/DuckDB.
Specimen, result and report references and literals were checked.
All three views were saved and tables compared with both engines.
The interpretation distinguishes specimen, observation, report and view rows.
questions: Why does the report-reference table contain more rows than reports?
Which parts of this case would require new decisions for another SQL source?
r.expected: The example produces five resources of four types: Patient, Specimen, two Observation and DiagnosticReport. Together with the core case it covers seven constructor types; it is not seven resources in one file. One specimen/report, two observations and two result rows. Literals 5.00/72.00/13.50; lower boundaries 4.995/71.995/13.495. Compare specimens, observations and results with both engines.
r.evidence: Laboratory NDJSON, three JSON view definitions, compared tables and participant explanation.
r.mistakes: Confusing seven types across cases with seven laboratory resources; omitting a view; assuming profile validation.

fhir.title: Define interoperability scope and candidate identity
fhir.goal: Delimit the claims this session can support and prepare a reproducible environment.
steps: Agree on FHIR participant profile, technical level, core/seven scope and interoperability questions. Record FHIR, R, SQL, profile and terminology experience separately.
Check candidate identity and open the isolated library using LEEME.en.md; record R assistance separately from semantic defects.
Read the five checks and distinguish local construction, table comparison, profile validation and human evaluation. Record DBI/recovery exclusions at basic level.
Identify the supplied base-profile/HAPI evidence as prior evidence and state which checks of your own environment are outside this session.
checks: Identity, environment, level and agreed scope were recorded.
Installation was checked and assistance described.
Checking layers and their evidence were distinguished.
Unevaluated profiles and servers were stated explicitly.
questions: What does the local constructor check, and what requires profile or terminology validation?
What evidence would you request to claim interoperability with a specific system?
fhir.expected: R4 4.0.1, candidate 0.5.0.9002 identified by commit and SHA-256. HAPI CI is prior maintainer evidence, not a participant execution. A local pass or 144/144 view-suite result does not validate national profiles, terminology or reference existence.
fhir.evidence: Identity/environment, reports consulted and a written checked/not-evaluated matrix.
fhir.mistakes: Using view conformance as general FHIR certification; claiming the participant ran HAPI after reading a report.
fhir.code:
source("INICIAR.R")
iniciar_piloto("completo", "sesion-P02-intento01")
abrir_sesion("sesion-P02-intento01")
packageVersion("fhirviews")
find.package("fhirviews")
help("fhir_mapa", package = "fhirviews")
browseVignettes("fhirviews")

fhir.title: Review mappings, cardinalities and semantic decisions
fhir.goal: Distinguish base-model rules, constructor contract and source decisions.
steps: Review maps in r4-estabilidad.R and the resulting resources. Relate columns, constants and references to concrete JSON destinations.
For Patient, Encounter, Condition, Observation and Immunization, create a field/source-or-constant/base-or-constructor requirement/project-decision matrix.
Check at least Encounter status/class, Condition subject, Observation status/code and Immunization patient/vaccineCode/occurrence using the help and agreed R4 model.
Explain a constant that cannot automatically transfer to another source and why a ViewDefinition is not a complete inverse map.
checks: The matrix distinguishes columns, constants and references.
Base requirements, invariants/profiles and local contract were separated.
Semantic decisions requiring project agreement were identified.
The limits of reconstruction from a tabular projection were explained.
questions: Why does the constructor requiring id not mean every FHIR resource must already have it before creation?
Is it valid to assume status=final for every source because the example uses it?
fhir.expected: The constructor requires a unique id per row by contract. Encounter requires status/class; Condition requires subject in the base; Observation status/code; Immunization status/vaccineCode/patient/one occurrence alternative. Invariants/profiles may require more. Example constants are explicit decisions, not clinical inference. Maps use JSON paths such as valueQuantity.value, not FHIRPath.
fhir.evidence: Per-resource matrix with versioned documentary sources and decision rationale.
fhir.mistakes: Confusing the id contract with base cardinality; inventing codes/status; treating a snapshot as the entire profile.

fhir.title: Audit types, choices, dates and precision
fhir.goal: Check that transformation preserves meaning and rejects incompatible alternatives.
steps: Compare FALSE, absence and i1/i2 texts against NDJSON and views. Identify occurrence[x] and doseNumber[x] by their JSON names and types.
Inspect the JSON literals 72.00/0.50 and computed boundaries; explain the risk of SQL DECIMAL→double before mapping.
In a separate fictional script, try Patient.active="false", an impossible date and an Immunization with both occurrence alternatives. Record rejections with class and field when known.
Explain partial date/Date versus an instant with timezone and why hours, quantities or absent fields must not be filled in for convenience.
checks: Present values and missing fields were checked without invented conversions.
Choice alternatives and scale were checked in the exact source.
All three invalid cases were rejected and diagnostics retained.
The participant explained dates and precision with their limitations.
questions: Do the literals 72 and 72.00 provide the same precision evidence?
What semantic harm could result from replacing an unknown date with an invented date?
fhir.expected: active="false" is not boolean; 2025-02-29 is invalid; simultaneous occurrenceDateTime/occurrenceString are exclusive choices. Expect fhirviews_error_mapeo. FALSE remains present, absent alternatives are omitted/NA, and 72.00/0.50 retain boundaries 71.995/0.495. A date without time is not an instant; issued requires an instant with timezone.
fhir.evidence: Choice matrix, NDJSON fragments, script and negative-case diagnostics.
fhir.mistakes: Checking precision only in R printing; converting text to boolean automatically; inventing timezone/time.

fhir.title: Check references and graph integrity
fhir.goal: Distinguish permitted target, constructed key and existence of the referenced resource.
steps: Draw or tabulate links among the six core resources. Identify type/id, patient references and encounter relationships.
Check that each local reference resolves to the expected resource by type and id; record absent optional links.
Create one negative case targeting Group from Immunization.patient and another using a syntactically valid patient id absent from the dataset. Compare behavior.
Explain handling of duplicate ids across servers, absolute references, URNs and persistence dependencies; identify what the local constructor does not check.
checks: The case’s links were checked by type and id.
Optional absences were retained and explained.
Incompatible target rejection and an unresolved reference were contrasted.
Structural validation was distinguished from existence/resolution.
questions: Can Patient/nonexistent pass the constructor? What remains to be checked?
Is id p1 sufficient to join resources from two different servers?
fhir.expected: Group as an Immunization.patient target is rejected. Patient/no-existe can be structurally admissible while absent from the dataset; existence needs an additional check. Condition/c1 and Immunization/i1 link Encounter/e1; i2 has no encounter. Server provenance prevents confusing equal ids from different sources.
fhir.evidence: Link inventory, both-case script and rejection/unresolved-reference evidence.
fhir.mistakes: Confusing allowed type with existence; resolving by position; ignoring id provenance.

fhir.title: Examine bindings and Coding fidelity
fhir.goal: Check vocabulary selection without treating labels or partial lists as full validation.
steps: Inspect clinicalStatus/verificationStatus Coding in the allergy example. Identify canonical system, code, display and additional translations.
Check the Coding selected by the view and that system/code/display belong to the same entry. Inspect the Coding entry without a code.
Create two fictional Patient cases separately: valid and invalid gender. Record rejection of the enumerable required binding and explain why this does not validate any clinical terminology.
List systems/ValueSets/versions needed for your environment, distinguishing required/extensible bindings and example data. Server terminology queries remain outside scope unless agreed.
checks: Coding entries were reviewed as coherent system/code pairs.
Canonical states and translations were checked without mixing entries.
The enumerable required binding rejected the invalid code.
External terminology and project profiles remained explicit requirements.
questions: Can display be used as a stable concept identifier?
Why does a partial code list or code.text not demonstrate a complete required binding?
fhir.expected: a1 contains the translation activo and canonical code active; the view selects by system. For a3, do not combine urn:ejemplo:primero with NO-MEZCLAR from another entry. Invalid Patient.gender is rejected. Extensible bindings are not closed enumerations; external/filtered ValueSets require agreed terminology services.
fhir.evidence: Checked Coding table, negative case and project terminology requirements.
fhir.mistakes: Mixing system/code/display across entries; validating by display; closing an extensible binding.

fhir.title: Audit the projection and its information loss
fhir.goal: Assess whether views retain sufficient relationships for the declared use.
steps: Create and save an Immunization view with patient and both occurrence alternatives; justify keys, types and omitted columns.
Run the allergy view and check reaction/manifestation relationships, categories as lists and records without reactions.
Compare rows, distinct ids and row meaning; identify an extraction that could introduce false associations or overcounting.
At full level, compare equivalent V8/DuckDB tables by keys, values and types. At basic level, leave engine comparison not evaluated; explain the conformance suite’s scope.
checks: The saved definition and information loss were explained.
Reaction/manifestation relationships and rows without reactions were checked.
Rows and resources were distinguished without artificial associations.
Engine comparison was documented according to technical level.
questions: What information beyond this view would you need to reconstruct the original resource?
Does passing the test suite imply that any FHIRPath can be translated to SQL?
fhir.expected: Immunization retains i1/i2 and missing alternatives as NA; allergies has three records/five rows with manifestations tied to their reactions. A view can lose information. 144/144 applies to the fixed suite; DuckDB retains a documented subset and does not accept every expression.
fhir.evidence: Participant ViewDefinition, audit table and engine comparison or justified exclusion.
fhir.mistakes: Treating extraction as reversible conversion; ignoring types; extrapolating the suite to all FHIRPath.

fhir.title: Design validation against environment profiles
fhir.goal: Produce a reviewable interoperability plan without claiming unperformed executions.
steps: For each resource in scope, list base profile, project profile if any, FHIR version, terminology and references needing resolution.
Review supplied HAPI evidence as prior maintainer evidence and distinguish it from participant execution. Record remaining project invariants/requirements.
Define a future trial or, only if a test server was agreed, run $validate on exact JSON retaining canonical profile, server/version, date, HTTP status and OperationOutcome.

Include a valid resource and an altered resource that must be rejected. For an executed server trial classify valid/rejected/indeterminate and review warnings; otherwise leave profile validation not evaluated.
checks: A per-resource profile/version/requirements matrix exists.
Maintainer evidence was separated from participant execution.
The plan includes positive/negative cases and interpretation rules.
External validation status was recorded without approving unexecuted checks.
questions: What does valido=NA or an incomplete OperationOutcome mean?
Why does declaring meta.profile not itself prove conformance with that profile?
fhir.expected: The required task is completed by producing and explaining the plan; a server execution is an optional extension. No network/server is required for the core. $validate HTTP errors or incomplete responses are indeterminate; warnings need review. No production resources are saved/sent. A base-profile pass does not demonstrate a national profile pass.
fhir.evidence: Validation matrix/plan; for an agreed execution, exact JSON and reviewed OperationOutcome with date/profile/server.
fhir.mistakes: Marking profiles passed because a plan was written; treating NA as TRUE; executing against production without agreement.

fhir.title: Repeat the audit and issue a bounded conclusion
fhir.goal: Check repetition, review findings and decide what interoperability was evaluated.
steps: Repeat the installed trial in a new directory and a manual references/Coding/choices audit without hints; identify repeated tasks and retain both evidence sets.
Compare findings and record data/type/interpretation discrepancies separately from environment differences. Correct and retest critical/high issues before favorable closure.
Answer the interview: hardest mapping decision, missing information for your environment, confidence reviewing results and up to three priority improvements.
Participant and maintainer review scope, unexecuted profiles, assistance, owners and human decision; export records and review attachments.
checks: The second attempt was retained and manual-repeat scope identified.
Findings were compared and discrepancies recorded.
The conclusion distinguishes structure, semantics, profiles and usefulness.
Both people reviewed the export, priorities and follow-up.
questions: Which interoperability claim can this session support, and which requires another test?
Would you recommend this path for an integration trial, and under which concrete conditions?
fhir.expected: Technical results remain separate from human and profile decisions. Favorable closure requires completed in-scope tasks, correct understanding and no open critical/high issues. Independence is limited to tasks repeated with evidence and zero interventions; it does not automatically extend to the entire profile.
fhir.evidence: Two attempts, repeated audit, exported record and conclusion identifying pending scope.
fhir.mistakes: Generalizing to other servers/profiles; confusing R assistance with FHIR defects; claiming global independence without repeating every task.

fhir.title: Audit Specimen and DiagnosticReport end to end
fhir.goal: Complete semantic review of the two additional constructors under seven-type scope.
steps: Confirm full level and run laboratorio-r4.R with fictional data. Identify maps, queries, types and generated resources.
Audit the Patient→Specimen/Observation/DiagnosticReport graph and result[].reference/specimen[].reference collections; check all references by type and id.

Check required DiagnosticReport status/code, base optionality of subject and Specimen status/subject, issued timezone and quantity precision. Separately test invalid status and result targeting the wrong type.
Save all three views, exact NDJSON and V8/DuckDB comparisons; add these types to the F07 plan. Under core scope, justify not evaluated without claiming seven-type review.
checks: Laboratory maps and graph were audited with all links.
Base cardinalities were distinguished from project requirements.
Both invalid cases were rejected and precision checked.
All three views/engines and profile requirements were documented.
questions: Must every Specimen have a Patient subject in base R4?
What prevents a structurally valid reference from resolving to the wrong result in another source?
fhir.expected: Five resources/four types in the laboratory extend joint coverage to seven constructor types. Specimen can have an environmental subject and base status/subject are optional; DiagnosticReport requires status/code, not subject; issued is an instant with timezone. The report references two Observation and one Specimen. Reject invalid status and result targeting Patient. All three views must match in V8/DuckDB; HAPI/project profiles remain separate.
fhir.evidence: Graph, field matrix, NDJSON, negative diagnostics, three views and compared tables.
fhir.mistakes: Always requiring Patient for an environmental specimen; confusing structural references with resolution; claiming profile validation from table comparison.
